extracted.intended_audience: readers of historical/biographical criticism; educated general public interested in Francis Bacon and judicial morality
extracted.subtask_description: A critical historical essay assessing the public conduct and moral character of Francis Bacon, especially his behaviour as a judge and minister, and analysing attempts to defend him. Emphasises standards for judicial integrity, contemporary moral opinion, and how to weigh defenses based on custom or political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial impartiality / no private solicitations
rubrics_metrics.description: “A judge who listens to private solicitations is a disgrace to his post.” Bacon himself had warned Villiers against interposing in causes depending in any court of justice; yet as Lord Keeper he allowed Buckingham to interfere and suffered Buckingham to dictate many of his decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper judge must refuse private solicitations and not allow friends or patrons to influence outcomes. Example/anti-pattern: Bacon’s permitting Buckingham’s interference in Chancery suits is presented as a clear violation of duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of presents from suitors constitutes corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon “and his dependants accepted large presents from persons who were engaged in Chancery suits.” Specific cases alleged include Aubrey (a hinted 100 pounds) and Egerton (a present of four hundred pounds) where promises of expedition were made but decrees were unfavourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving gifts from parties before the court is a substantive ground for judging misconduct. The essay treats such largesse as illicit gains even if the exact amount proved at trial was uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid even the appearance of bias; appearance leaves a taint of suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the judge be so just, and of such courage as he ought to be, as not to be inclined thereby, yet it always leaves a taint of suspicion behind it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a judge resists being influenced, association with solicitations or gifts damages reputation and public confidence. Evaluations should account for both actual partiality and the corrosive effect of appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of an immoral practice is not a defence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The circumstance that a great many people are in the habit of committing immoral actions is no plea at all.” The author concedes that judges taking gifts was common, but insists that commonness does not excuse wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical misconduct, distinguish frequency from moral acceptability: the mere fact many did it does not absolve an individual. Analogy used: many thieves do not excuse a caught shop-breaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary moral condemnation as evidence of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay cites Hugh Latimer’s sermons (pre-dating Bacon) that denounce bribery in strong terms—calling bribery “a princely kind of thieving” and urging punitive imagery—showing that such practices were publicly condemned before Bacon’s punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate whether a practice was morally accepted in its time, look for contemporaneous voices and public opinion. Latimer’s invectives are offered as proof that bribery was already regarded as odious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of a guilty plea should be weighed against available defense and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay argues Bacon’s repeated, signed, and acted-upon confession (his paper, his plea on the thirtieth, and submission to sentence) is credible: “He plainly and ingenuously confess that I am guilty of corruption… it is my act, my hand, my heart.” The author finds Montagu’s claim that this was a forced falsehood implausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a confession is genuine or coerced, consider whether the accused had realistic means or motive to defend himself, whether he persisted in and authenticated the confession, and whether political actors would have prevented a successful defense if it existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not excuse misconduct by attributing it to lack of intelligence or experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Neither on this occasion nor on any other could his bad actions be attributed to any defect of the head. They sprang from quite a different cause.” Bacon’s misdeeds are presented as deliberate, not merely errors of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating wrongdoing by a seasoned public figure, one should favour explanations rooted in motive and moral failing rather than incompetence, especially when the subject is experienced and intellectually able.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the culpability of enablers and the political context
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay holds that those who place impulsive, ill-informed youths in power (e.g., Buckingham) bear responsibility for resulting abuses: “Those who intrust a petulant, hot-blooded, ill-informed lad with power, are more to blame than he for the mischief.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should allocate blame not only to the actor but also to patrons, advisors, and systems that enable misconduct. Contextual political dynamics (patronage networks, royal favour) are relevant to judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing and punishment can be partly performative and politically symbolic
rubrics_metrics.description: “The sentence was, however, severe--the more severe, no doubt, because the Lords knew that it would not be executed, and that they had an excellent opportunity of exhibiting, at small cost, the inflexibility of their justice, and their abhorrence of corruption.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting the severity of penalties, consider political signalling: a harsh sentence may be intended to display institutional virtue rather than to assure practical punishment. This matters for assessing proportionality and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive arguments must distinguish cause from effect and avoid logical reversals
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticises Mr. Montagu for ‘mistak[ing] effect for cause,’ e.g., arguing that Bacon did not defend himself because he was not supported by the Court, when in fact the Court did not support him because he could not convincingly defend himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing or evaluating biographies/defenses, ensure causal claims are sound: do not treat consequences as explanations for the antecedent facts. Check whether alleged motives or pressures plausibly explain behaviour rather than reverse causation.
